content: Bipedalism refers to the ability to stand or move on two appendages, typically the legs, and includes activities such as walking, running, or hopping. Animals or machines that primarily use bipedal locomotion are called bipeds, a term derived from the Latin words bi (two) and ped (foot). Types of Bipedal Movement 1. Standing: This involves remaining stationary on both legs. For most bipeds, maintaining balance while standing is an active process requiring constant adjustments. 2. Walking: This is characterized by placing one foot in front of the other, ensuring that at least one foot is always in contact with the ground. 3. Running: In this form of movement, one foot is placed in front of the other, but there are moments when both feet are off the ground simultaneously. 4. Hopping: This involves a series of jumps where both feet move together. Bipedal Animals Bipedal locomotion has evolved multiple times across different species, particularly among vertebrates. Birds and their theropod dinosaur ancestors are the most prominent examples. All dinosaurs are believed to have descended from a fully bipedal ancestor, possibly resembling Eoraptor. Among modern birds, large flightless species like ostriches epitomize bipedal efficiency, capable of reaching speeds up to 65 km/h. Similarly, many theropod dinosaurs, such as maniraptors, likely achieved comparable speeds. Bipedalism also re-evolved in other dinosaur lineages, such as the iguanodons. Some extinct crocodilian relatives, like Effigia okeeffeae from the Triassic period, also exhibited bipedalism. Among birds, larger species tend to walk with alternating legs, while smaller birds often hop. Penguins are unique in their upright posture, which contrasts with the horizontal body orientation of most other birds. Bipedalism is less common among mammals, most of which are quadrupedal. The largest group of bipedal mammals includes kangaroos and their relatives, which primarily move by hopping. Other hopping mammals include kangaroo rats and springhares. Certain primates, such as sifakas and sportive lemurs, also hop when on the ground. Gibbons and giant pangolins are among the few mammals, aside from humans, that commonly use an alternating bipedal gait rather than hopping. Some mammals exhibit limited bipedalism. For instance, bonobos and proboscis monkeys, which inhabit flooded forests, wade through water in a bipedal stance. Occasionally, these primates, along with others, may walk or stand bipedally on land. Other animals, like rats, squat on their hind legs to manipulate food, while raccoons often stand erect in water to use their hands for handling objects. Beavers may move bipedally when carrying branches, and bears may rise and move bipedally during confrontations to better use their forelimbs as weapons. Ground squirrels and meerkats stand on their hind legs to survey their surroundings but do not walk bipedally. Gerenuk antelopes stand on their hind legs to browse leaves from trees, a behavior also observed in the extinct giant ground sloth and possibly in chalicotheres. The spotted skunk adopts a unique form of bipedalism by standing on its forelimbs when threatened, allowing it to aim its anal glands at attackers while maintaining eye contact. Bipedalism is virtually absent among amphibians. Among non-archosaur reptiles, it is rare but can be observed in certain lizards that rear up to run. For example, some basilisk lizards can run across water surfaces using this method. Insects like cockroaches also exhibit bipedal running in specific situations, but bipedal movement is otherwise unknown in arthropods. While most bipeds are terrestrial, at least two species of octopus have been observed walking bipedally on the seafloor, using the tips of two arms. This form of locomotion may allow them to remain camouflaged while moving quickly, as the remaining six arms can be used for disguise, mimicking objects like coconuts or seaweed. The walking movements are thought to require minimal brain control. Exceptional Cases Many animals that do not naturally use bipedal locomotion can be trained to walk on their hind legs. Animals with limb injuries or congenital deformities may adapt to bipedal motion, either on two hind legs or on one front and one back leg. For example, some dogs have been observed walking bipedally due to such adaptations. Certain individual primates have also been known to adopt bipedalism. One notable case is a captive macaque named Natasha, who switched to bipedal walking entirely after recovering from a severe illness. Another example is a captive chimpanzee named Oliver, who exclusively walked upright. Some animals can also be trained to walk on their front limbs, and humans can learn to walk using only their arms, as seen in handstands and hand-walking. Advantages of Bipedalism Bipedalism offers several evolutionary advantages: 1. Improved Perception: Standing upright enhances the ability to detect distant dangers or resources, which may have been a crucial stage in the evolution of bipedal species. 2. Free Forelimbs: In vertebrates, bipedalism frees the front limbs for other functions, such as manipulation (in primates), flight (in birds), digging (in pangolins), or combat (in bears). 3. Wading: Some animals, like raccoons and primates, adopt a bipedal stance in water, allowing them to stand or walk in deeper water while breathing air. 4. Faster Movement: In animals with inflexible backbones, such as lizards or cockroaches, bipedalism can increase running speed. However, the maximum speed of bipedal movement is generally slower than that of quadrupedal movement with a flexible backbone. For example, the fastest biped, the ostrich, can reach 65 km/h, while the cheetah, a quadruped, can achieve 103 km/h. 5. Greater Reach: Gerenuk antelopes use a bipedal stance to access leaves from trees. 6. Camouflage: Bipedalism in octopuses may allow them to move while keeping the rest of their bodies still for camouflage. 7. Defensive Posture: The spotted skunk's bipedal stance allows it to face attackers while directing its anal glands at them, which can spray a foul-smelling oil. Evolution of Bipedalism Bipedalism has evolved independently in various lineages due to its adaptive advantages. Early Reptiles and Lizards The earliest known biped is Eudibamus cursoris, a bolosaurid reptile from 290 million years ago. Its long hind legs, short forelegs, and distinctive joints suggest bipedalism, which may have increased its speed. This species became extinct before the appearance of dinosaurs. Independently, some modern lizards have developed the ability to run on their hind legs for added speed. Dinosaurs and Birds Bipedalism evolved independently among dinosaurs, which diverged from their archosaur ancestors around 230 million years ago during the Triassic period. Fossils of early dinosaurs like Eoraptor suggest that the first dinosaurs were small, bipedal predators. Primitive dinosaur-like ornithodirans, such as Marasuchus and Lagerpeton, also support this view. Mammals (Excluding Humans) Many mammals adopt a bipedal stance in specific situations, such as feeding or fighting. Some groups, like kangaroos and giant pangolins, have independently evolved bipedalism as their primary form of locomotion. Kangaroos are believed to have developed bipedal hopping at least 45 million years ago. Humans The evolution of bipedalism in humans is a complex process with at least twelve distinct hypotheses explaining its origins. Evidence suggests that bipedalism evolved before the expansion of human brain size. Various selective forces likely acted together to drive the evolution of human bipedalism.
